title: Solve Multiple Equations With List Regression
description: Pair equation sides in equal-length lists to solve systems, combine function conditions, apply restrictions, and find fixed ratios using a legal free base.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep your first idea, even if you are unsure. You can continue without submitting an answer.

shared_prompt.title: Opening question
shared_prompt.html: The function \(h\) is defined by \(h(x)=a(x-3)^2+b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. If \(h(1)=26\) and \(a+b=11\), what is the value of \(a-b\)?

blocks.html:
Let one regression connect the conditions

The opening question gives two conditions about the same constants. Solving each separately would miss that connection.

List regression asks Desmos to match several pairs of expressions at once. We’ll start with two simple equations so you can see how to enter the pairs.

content.prompt: Which pair satisfies both original equations?
content.explanation: The readout gives \(a=7\) and \(b=4\): their sum is 11 and their difference is 3. The pair must satisfy both conditions.
content.hint: Check the sum and the difference of the same pair.

blocks.html:
Match the positions

A system is a group of equations that must hold together. For \(a+b=11\) and \(a-b=3\), \([a+b,a-b]\sim[11,3]\) matches first to first and second to second.

content.explanation: The first entries encode \(2m+n=17\); the second encode \(m-n=4\). Reversing just the right list would attach each expression to the wrong number.
content.hint: Read the first entries as one equation, then the second entries as another.

blocks.html:
Pair the Sides

  1. Put each left side in one list and its matching right side in the other.
  2. Type one tilde, ~, between the lists.
  3. Read the unknowns and inspect the fit.
  4. Calculate what the question asks for.

For unknowns named \(x,y\), use uppercase \(X,Y\). Lowercase \(x,y\) have graphing jobs in Desmos.

content.prompt: Which entry uses list regression for \(x+y=12\) and \(x-2y=3\)?
content.explanation: Use uppercase \(X,Y\), keep the matching sides together, and connect the lists with \(\sim\). Report the result using the original \(x,y\).
content.hint: Check the letter case, the tilde, and which entries are paired.

blocks.html:
Check that the conditions match

RMSE measures the gap between the paired sides. For exact equations, it should be zero or tiny. A noticeable gap means the displayed values do not solve the entered system; recheck the setup.

Use the resulting values in another row when the question asks for an expression such as \(2a+b\). Regression finds one solution; it does not establish how many solutions exist.

content.title: Build the paired lists
content.instructions_html: Enter \(2u+v=19\) and \(u-v=2\) as one list regression. Keep matching sides in the same positions. Read \(u,v\) and inspect RMSE.

feedback.success_message_html: Nice work! The conditions are paired correctly. Desmos fits \(u=7\) and \(v=5\).
feedback.retry_message_html: Use one row with two square-bracket lists and one tilde. Keep each complete side as written, and check which entries line up.
feedback.solution_html: Enter \([2u+v,u-v]\sim[19,2]\). Desmos shows \(u=7\) and \(v=5\); the paired values match with zero or tiny RMSE.

content.explanation: Typing \(3u-v\) gives \(16\). The SAT asked for the expression, not either value.
content.hint: Use the two values in the requested expression.
content.solution:
Keep the values available, or enter them in this scratch calculator as \(u=7\) and \(v=5\).
Type \(3u-v\). The result is \(16\).

blocks.html:
A function definition keeps its equals sign

Suppose \(f(x)=a(x-2)^2+b\), with \(f(0)=17\) and \(a+b=8\). Define \(f(x)\) on one row. Then pair the conditions: \([f(0),a+b]\sim[17,8]\).

The input \(x\) can stay lowercase inside the definition. The unknown constants here are \(a,b\).

One result may not be the only result

For \(r+s=13\) and \(rs=40\), both \((8,5)\) and \((5,8)\) work. Regression may show either pair. Use graphing or algebra when the question asks for all solutions or their count.

content.explanation: The swapped pair \((5,8)\) also satisfies both equations. A successful fit establishes a working pair, not the number of pairs.
choices: The other pair has a larger RMSE.
The solution count is the displayed RMSE.
This pair works; another pair can also work.
content.hint: Compare what happens when the two values trade places.

blocks.html:
Include a stated restriction

If the question also says \(r>s\), put that condition in braces after the right list:

\[[r+s,rs]\sim[13,40]\{r>s\}\]

That selects the allowed pair. Include restrictions the question gives; do not invent one to force a preferred answer.

shared_prompt.title: Relative weights question
shared_prompt.html: A sample’s weight \(A\) is \(240\%\) of weight \(B\), and \(A\) is \(0.8\%\) of weight \(C\). The question asks: \(C\) is what percent \(p\) of \(B\)?

blocks.html:
Set a scale when only ratios are given

Here the sample weights are related by ratios, and the question asks for a percent. Choosing \(B=1\) preserves those ratios.

Define \(B=1\), then enter \([A,A,C]\sim[2.4B,0.008C,(p/100)B]\). This connects all three statements at once.

content.prompt: In that relative-weight problem, why can you define \(B=1\)?
content.explanation: Changing the common weight scale preserves the percent comparisons. Choose B; the equations determine the corresponding A and C.
choices: The requested percent fixes B at one gram.
Scaling the weights together preserves their ratios.
Regression requires the letter B to equal one.
One equation lets you choose every weight separately.
content.hint: Ask whether multiplying all three weights by the same positive factor changes any comparison.

blocks.html:
Keep zero from erasing the comparison

If all three weights are free, \(A=B=C=0\) satisfies the entered equations for any \(p\). That result cannot tell you the requested percent. Setting the free base \(B=1\) removes this zero-weight case.

content.prompt: What is the percent \(p\) of weight \(B\) that equals weight \(C\)?
content.explanation: With \(B=1\), the regression gives \(A=2.4,C=300,p=30000\). A multiplier of 300 is 30,000 percent, so report \(30000\).
content.hint: Fix the free base, then include the requested percent as the third paired condition.
content.solution:
Enter \(B=1\).
Enter \([A,A,C]\sim[2.4B,0.008C,(p/100)B]\).
Read the fitted parameter \(p=30000\). The value \(C=300\) is the multiplier, not the percent.

blocks.html:
Keep any supplied measurement

If the question gives \(B=75\) grams, use \(B=75\). Choosing a base works when only relative amounts matter. It cannot determine an actual weight from ratios alone.

content.prompt: A problem states that sample B weighs 75 grams. What should replace the base definition from the previous example?
content.explanation: Keep the supplied measurement. Choosing a different base here would change the actual-weight problem.
content.hint: Distinguish a free reference scale from a measurement supplied in the question.

blocks.html:
The same pairing works with powers

For the power equations in the prompt, pair complete sides: \([p^{3/4},t]\sim[t^{5/2},p^{2n-1}]\{p>1\}\{t>1\}\).

Put each restriction after the right list. They exclude \(p=t=1\), which would make both equations true without determining \(n\).

content.prompt: Why would allowing \(p=t=1\) fail to determine \(n\) in the power equations?
content.explanation: Both sides become 1 regardless of \(n\). The problem excludes that case with \(p>1,t>1\).
choices: The first equation would have a negative side.
The second equation would force n to be 1.
The two lists would have different lengths.
content.hint: Evaluate a few different powers with base 1.

blocks.html:
Choose a free base that preserves the target

These power relationships give the same \(n\) for each allowed \(p>1\). Define \(p=2\), then enter \([p^{3/4},t]\sim[t^{5/2},p^{2n-1}]\{t>1\}\).

Read \(n\). The chosen base simplifies the fit while keeping the requested exponent fixed.

content.prompt: What value of \(n\) does the regression give for these power equations?
content.explanation: The fit gives \(n=0.65=13/20\). Changing the legal base changes \(t\), while this value of \(n\) stays the same.
content.hint: Use a legal fixed p and enter both full power expressions in matching positions.
content.solution:
Enter \(p=2\).
Enter \([p^{3/4},t]\sim[t^{5/2},p^{2n-1}]\{t>1\}\).
Read \(n=0.65\). Enter \(13/20\) to confirm the same decimal.

blocks.html:
Keep the unknowns free

Use one regression for the connected conditions. Separate regression rows do not connect to each other.

If an unknown already has a slider or definition, remove it so regression can find it. Recheck pairing, restrictions, and RMSE if the result does not fit the problem.

Return to the function

Try the opening question again. Decide how to combine its conditions, then find the quantity it asks for.

content.prompt: Return to the opening question. What answer do you get now?
content.explanation: Define \(h(x)=a(x-3)^2+b\), then enter \([h(1),a+b]\sim[26,11]\). The values are \(a=5,b=6\). Typing \(a-b\) gives \(-1\).
content.hint: Define h(x), then pair h(1)=26 and a+b=11 in one regression. Use the resulting a and b to evaluate a-b.
content.solution: Define \(h(x)=a(x-3)^2+b\), then enter \([h(1),a+b]\sim[26,11]\). The values are \(a=5,b=6\). Typing \(a-b\) gives \(-1\).

content.prompt: Two equations, two unknowns. Recall “pair the sides”: how do you build the regression and finish?
content.explanation: Matching positions preserve the equations. The tilde fits their unknowns together; the conditions and requested quantity decide what you report.
choices: Pair left sides with right sides in matching order; use = between the lists; check conditions and evaluate the requested quantity.
Pair left sides with right sides in separate orders; use ~ between the lists; check conditions and evaluate the requested quantity.
Pair left sides with right sides in matching order; use ~ between the lists; report RMSE as the requested quantity.
Pair left sides with right sides in matching order; use ~ between the lists; check conditions and evaluate the requested quantity.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=c(x-1)^2+d\). If \(g(3)=22\) and \(c+d=10\), what is \(c\)?
content.explanation: Define \(g\), then enter \([g(3),c+d]\sim[22,10]\). Desmos fits \(c=4,d=6\). Report \(4\).

content.prompt: The positive numbers \(m,n\) satisfy \(m+n=15\) and \(mn=54\). If \(m<n\), what is \(m\)?
content.explanation: Enter \([m+n,mn]\sim[15,54]\{m<n\}\). The values are \(m=6,n=9\), consistent with the positive-number condition.

content.prompt: The mass of sample R is 360% of the mass of sample S and 0.9% of the mass of sample T. If the mass of sample T is \(q\%\) of the mass of sample S, what is the value of \(q\)?
content.explanation: Define \(S=1\), then enter \([R,R,T]\sim[3.6S,0.009T,(q/100)S]\). Desmos fits \(R=3.6,T=400,q=40000\). The requested percent is \(40000\), not the multiplier \(400\).

content.html:
Pair the sides

Keep the related conditions together in one regression.
